t: The movement was launched by the writers of New Youth, who blamed Confucian culture for China's weakness and called for “Mr. Science” and “Mr. Democracy” in its place.
Hu Shih's argument that “a dead language cannot produce a living literature” led to the written vernacular, baihuawen, replacing Literary Chinese in literature.
The protest of 4 May 1919 turned a cultural movement into a political one, and its leaders then split: Hu Shih urged a return to study, while Chen Duxiu and Li Dazhao turned to organised politics.
dyk: The first vernacular Chinese fiction was Chen Hengzhe's short story One Day, published in 1917, a year before Lu Xun's Diary of a Madman, which has often been incorrectly credited as the first.
ev: Zhang Shizhao founds the political magazine The Tiger in Tokyo; it runs until October 1915
Chen Duxiu founds the Youth Magazine, later retitled New Youth, marking the beginning of the movement
Hu Shih publishes Preliminary Discussion on Literary Reform in New Youth, urging writers not to imitate the ancients
Lu Xun publishes Diary of a Madman, which implies that China's traditional culture was mentally cannibalistic
Students in Beijing protest the transfer of German rights over Jiaozhou Bay to Japan, and the movement becomes political
The death of the student Li Chao becomes a rallying cry for anti-feudal and feminist agitation
New Culture reformers welcome Margaret Sanger's visit to China, and Hu Shih translates her speech on birth control
Rabindranath Tagore lectures in China and warns that it could encounter trouble by integrating too much progressive and foreign thought

f.where: China, centred on Beijing, home of Peking University and Tsinghua University, and on Shanghai, with its flourishing publishing sector; some of its writers had first gathered in Tokyo
f.period: The Tiger published in Tokyo 1914–1915; New Youth founded 1915; Hu Shih's literary reform essay January 1917; May Fourth protest 1919; the movement split over politics from 1919; overwhelmed by the anti-imperialist and populist violence of the mid-1920s
f.figures: Chen Duxiu, founder of New Youth; Cai Yuanpei, chancellor of Peking University; Hu Shih, leader of the vernacular faction; Li Dazhao, librarian and editor; Lu Xun, author of Diary of a Madman; Gu Jiegang, historian of the Doubting Antiquity School; Chen Hengzhe, Bing Xin and Zhou Zuoren
f.outcome: the written vernacular spread and a new literature appeared, while the movement divided: Hu Shih and the liberals returned to scholarship, and Chen Duxiu and Li Dazhao took part in founding the Chinese Communist Party
